input.title: The Museum of Mystery Solids: Night Curator
input.designRationale: Reina is nine, has shown appetite for hard problems, notices logical inconsistencies, and responded well to clear examples and visible color. That evidence tells me two things I commit to: (1) she will tolerate a five-item sequence without candy-coated rewards if the fiction respects her intelligence, and (2) she will detect and resent fake feedback, so the design must be honest that no verdicts arrive until the end. I chose a 'night curator in a museum of solids' frame because a curator's job — examining objects and filing accurate records — makes withholding correctness feel natural and dignified rather than withheld: museum records are sealed until the ledger closes. That solves the hardest constraint (zero feedback, zero hints, zero teaching before commitment) narratively instead of mechanically. Every item is a pedestal exhibit; the child's job is to complete the exhibit's record card by selecting from fixed plaque options. Rotatable 3D-rendered solids (drag to orbit) directly serve C4: a child who can rotate the pyramid can discover the hidden square base by her own action, which is legitimate observation, not teaching — the contract measures reasoning about face composition, not memory of hidden faces, and orbiting is available identically on every item so it adds no differential exposure. The single permitted non-teaching clarification is embodied as a 'Reread the task' plaque button that only restates navigation/format ('Pick one card' / 'Pick every card that is true'), logged as hintRequested. The design deliberately refuses a score screen, stars, or mastery language; the payoff is the ledger closing and the museum lights coming on, reporting only factual completion.
independentlyChosenPrinciples: Honesty before charm: no interface element may imply correctness or incorrectness before the evaluation ends, and the fiction must make that silence feel purposeful, not withholding.
The child's hands should touch the mathematics: rotating the actual solid is the core physical act, so the evidence reflects 3D reasoning rather than picture-decoding skill.

Commitment is sacred: a response is only recorded when the child stamps the record card; everything before the stamp (selection, deselection, rotation) is exploration and is logged as option-change telemetry, never punished.
No trap states: skip is always visible, always neutral in tone, and never framed as failure ('Leave this exhibit for the day curator').

Reading is not the construct: prompts stay under 25 words, options are short cards with both a word and a small plane-figure glyph where the contract's options are shape names, and nothing requires typing.

Respect the observer: every logged key is factual (what was selected, when, after how many changes), and the closing report states attempts, assistance, exposure, friction, and completion — never mastery.
Color carries meaning only for attention, never for correctness: the highlighted face in I2 uses a single accent hue reserved exclusively for 'the surface being asked about'.
input.openingPromise: "The museum is dark. Five mystery solids arrived tonight, and their record cards are blank. You are the Night Curator — examine each one and file its true record before morning." One sentence, spoken and shown, over a dim gallery with five glowing pedestals.
input.firstThreeSeconds: Second 0–1: dim museum gallery fades in, five pedestals in a row, the nearest spotlit; a rotating cylinder/sphere/prism/cone quartet gleams on it. Second 1–2: a clipboard slides up from the bottom edge with the I1 prompt and four large option cards. Second 2–3: a soft pulsing halo on the nearest solid plus a one-line cue: "Drag a solid to turn it. Tap a card to answer." Nothing else moves; the required action is the only lit, pulsing thing on screen.
input.firstAction: Drag any of the four spotlit I1 solids to rotate it (optional exploration), then tap one of the four large option cards on the clipboard and press the big STAMP button to file the record. The stamp button is disabled-dim until a card is selected, so the causal chain (choose, then commit) is visible before any touch happens.
input.mission: Restore the Museum of Mystery Solids before the morning bell: five exhibits, five blank record cards. Each correctly examined-and-filed record card (filed, not judged — filing is completion, not correctness) advances the night clock and lights another wing of the museum. When the fifth card is stamped or set aside, the ledger seals, the lights come on, and the Night Curator's shift report is issued.
input.coreInteraction: Per exhibit: (1) read a short plaque prompt (≤25 words, also read aloud via a tap-to-listen speaker icon so reading is never the gate); (2) freely drag-rotate the pictured solid(s) in real 3D with momentum and snap-back, on touch or mouse; (3) tap option cards on the record clipboard — single-select items swap the selection, multi-select items toggle cards with a visible 'selected' pin, and I5's 'none of them' card auto-unpins all others with a visible animation so the exclusivity rule is shown, not read; (4) press STAMP to commit. The stamp is one large 96px target. After stamping, the pedestal's record slot fills with a wax-sealed card (contents hidden), the exhibit light dims to 'archived amber', and the walkway to the next pedestal illuminates. A 'Reread the task' button restates only the response format and navigation; it is logged as hintRequested and teaches nothing about flatness, faces, or shapes.
input.mathAsPower: The mathematics IS the curator's instrument: the only way to fill a record card truthfully is to reason about the solid's actual surfaces. Rotation makes face-set reasoning physically powerful — turning the square pyramid reveals the base a silhouette hides (C4), and turning the sphere shows there is nowhere flat to rest a card (C1/C3). The child's geometric judgment is what moves the night forward: each stamped record lights a wing of the museum, and no other action in the world does anything. There is no combat proxy, no timer proxy; discriminating flat from curved and naming face shapes is the sole lever of progress.
input.responseAffordances: All responses are large tap targets: option cards minimum 220×110px with generous spacing at 1365×768, stamp button 96px circular, skip link a full-width quiet bar. Single-select: tapping a card selects it and visibly deselects the previous one (swap animation), so changing one's mind is one tap. Multi-select: cards toggle with a pin/unpin animation; at least one pin required before STAMP enables (matching I3's rule); I5's exclusivity rule for 'none of them' is enforced by visible auto-unpinning. Every option card for shape-name options (I2, and the set descriptions in I4) carries a small monochrome plane-figure glyph beside the word so the answer does not depend on reading the word 'rectangle' — the glyph is a flat 2D icon, never a picture of the solid, so it cannot leak the answer. Tap-to-listen narration on every prompt and every option card. No typing, no dragging-to-precise-targets, no double-tap, no long-press, no keyboard. Rotation uses forgiving full-object hit areas. optionChangeCount is logged from card toggles before the stamp.
input.stakesAndConsequences: Stakes are diegetic and dignified: an unfiled record means a dark wing of the museum, and the morning bell fiction gives urgency without any actual timer (timeLimit is 'none' per contract; the clock advances only on stamps/skips, never on real time). Consequences of stamping are real and irreversible within the night — a stamped card is wax-sealed and cannot be reopened, which makes commitment meaningful and protects evidence independence. A skipped exhibit gets a visibly different 'day curator' tag, honestly recorded as noResponse. Nothing in the world ever labels a stamped card right or wrong; the stakes are about completing the shift truthfully, which is exactly what the instrument needs the child to believe.
input.recovery: No response can trap the child. Before stamping, any selection can be changed freely with single taps and is logged only as optionChangeCount. If the child stamps with an answer she is unsure of, the world reacts identically to any stamp — seal, amber light, walkway forward — so uncertainty is never exposed or punished. If she stalls, after 45 seconds of no input a gentle non-teaching nudge appears once per item: "Take your time. You can turn the solid, pick a card, or leave this one for the day curator." (navigation-only; logged as idleNudgeShown, distinct from hintRequested). Skip is always one tap and moves her forward with the same walkway animation. Accidental taps cannot commit anything because only STAMP commits. Early exit is available from a persistent quiet door icon: exiting mid-shift seals the ledger with reached items recorded and unreached items marked notAdministered, and the exit screen thanks the curator for the records filed — no failure framing.
input.progression: Fixed order I1→I5, presented as five pedestals along one gallery corridor, so progress is spatially legible: the child can always see how many exhibits remain by looking down the hall. A night-clock at the top advances one hour per terminal item (stamped or skipped), from 1am to 6am. Each completed exhibit lights its wing with a distinct architectural silhouette (rotunda, arch hall, glass atrium, stairwell, dome), giving a visible, non-evaluative progression reward. No difficulty is announced; the pedestals simply differ in what they hold, matching the contract's fixed item order and boundaries exactly.
input.worldReaction: Correct, incorrect, and uncertain stamps all produce the same truthful reaction: the wax seal presses down with a satisfying thunk, the card slides into the pedestal drawer, the exhibit dims to archived amber, the clock ticks one hour, and the next walkway lights. Changed selections before stamping produce a soft card-swap sound and pin animations — acknowledgment without judgment. A skip produces a gentler reaction: the card is clipped to the pedestal with a 'for the day curator' tag, same clock tick, same walkway. The rotation of solids gives continuous physical feedback (inertia, subtle specular highlights moving across flat faces as planes and across curved surfaces as sweeping bands — a truthful physical property of the render, present on every solid equally, not an added answer cue). Nothing ever glows green, buzzes red, or replays the item. Answer exposure is structurally impossible: sealed cards show only a seal.
input.payoff: At 6am the morning bell rings once, the gallery floods with warm daylight through the now-lit wings, and the ledger closes with a Shift Report the child can read: "Records filed: 4. Left for the day curator: 1. Times you asked to reread a task: 2. Museum wings lit: 5." Purely factual, no scores, no stars, no 'great job on shapes'. The emotional payoff is the transformation of the dark museum into a lit one by her own filed judgments, plus a curator's brass badge stamped with the night's date — a completion artifact, not a mastery award. A final line: "Your records are sealed for the Head Curator" honestly signals that evaluation happens elsewhere, later.
input.replayVariation: Replay never re-administers these five items — the contract's exposure identities are single-use evidence. A second visit offers a 'new shipment night' shell that is visibly different crates and pedestals but presents only whatever fresh item set the evidenceRequiredNext pipeline supplies (e.g., the no-sphere no-flat-face probe, the cylinder-vs-cone contrast); if no fresh instrument exists yet, replay is a non-evaluative free-rotation gallery where she can examine the archived solids with no questions, no records, and no new exposures — exploration only, logged as freePlay so it cannot contaminate the evidence trail. The museum shell, curator role, and controls carry over so re-onboarding cost is zero, but no evaluation exposure is ever reused.
input.visualDirection: Nocturne museum palette: deep indigo-charcoal walls, warm brass and parchment for the clipboard and cards, single spotlit pools of neutral white light on active exhibits so the solid's true colors and shading are uncontaminated. Solids are rendered in matte, clearly distinct mid-saturation hues (cylinder teal, sphere coral, prism ochre, cone violet, cube slate, pyramid sand) with soft ambient occlusion and a subtle ground shadow so 3D form reads instantly at 1365×768. The I2 highlighted top face uses one reserved accent — a luminous gold rim and fill on the top disc only — and that gold appears nowhere else in the entire experience. Perspective for the cylinder top is a gentle three-quarter view; the option glyph for 'circle' is a true circle, honestly leaving the ellipse-vs-circle labeling risk visible in the data rather than papering over it. Typography: a rounded, high-legibility sans at ≥22px for prompts, ≥20px on cards, high contrast on parchment. UI chrome is minimal: clipboard bottom third, gallery top two-thirds, clock top-center, skip bar and reread button quiet at the clipboard's edge.
input.motionDirection: Motion is calm and causal. Solids rotate under direct drag with light inertia and a slow idle auto-turn (one revolution per ~20s) so hidden faces eventually present themselves even to a child who never drags — equalizing exposure across children. Card selection: 150ms lift-and-pin. Stamp: 300ms press, seal squash, drawer slide — the one indulgent animation, reserved for commitment. Walkway lights ripple forward over 600ms to pull the eye to the next pedestal. No looping ambient animation competes with the solids; the gallery is still except for dust motes in spotlights. Idle nudge fades in/out gently. All motion respects reduced-motion settings by swapping to crossfades.
input.soundDirection: Sparse nocturne ambience: distant clock tick, soft room tone. Interaction sounds are informational and judgment-free: a low felt 'turn' sound while rotating, a paper tick on card pin/unpin, a warm wax 'thunk' on stamp (identical for every answer), a lighter paper clip sound on skip, a single hour chime as the clock advances, and one rising bell-and-birdsong swell at the 6am payoff. Tap-to-listen narration in a warm, unhurried adult voice reads prompts and option cards verbatim — narration is faithful text-to-audio, never explanatory, so it cannot become a content hint. No music stingers keyed to answers; no sound differs by correctness anywhere.
usefulLibraries: three.js (or react-three-fiber) for real-time rotatable solids with orbit controls constrained to rotation-only
GSAP for stamp/seal/walkway choreography with reduced-motion fallbacks
Howler.js for layered ambient and interaction audio with per-cue volume control
Pre-recorded human or high-quality TTS audio sprites for verbatim prompt/option narration (no runtime TTS variability)
Zustand or a tiny state machine (XState) to enforce the select→stamp commitment gate and terminal-state logging

A lightweight analytics event queue with local buffering for the measurement keys (selectedOption(Set), correct/exactSet, latencyMs, optionChangeCount, hintRequested, idleNudgeShown, skip, notAdministered)
anticipatedChildConfusions: 'Flat' misread as 'thin/lying down' (I1 confound): mitigated only by the honest picture and rotation — no verbal reteaching allowed; if she asks aloud, the reread button restates format only, and the risk stays logged.

I3/I5 multi-select treated as pick-one: Reina may assume one answer per card like I1/I2. Mitigation without teaching: the clipboard header changes from 'Pick one card' to 'Pick every card that is true' with a visibly different multi-pin tray; the reread button repeats exactly that sentence. Under-selection remains a live confound and is logged via partialCreditPattern.
I5 'none of them' interaction: she may not realize it clears other pins; the auto-unpin animation shows the rule the first time she taps it, before stamping, so no evidence is lost.

Cylinder top drawn as ellipse blocking the 'circle' card (I2): a child with strong perception may reject 'circle' as dishonest. I keep the true perspective render plus a true-circle glyph on the card and accept this as a contract-acknowledged unresolved risk.

Stamp finality anxiety: she may hesitate fearing wrongness. The idle nudge and the fiction ('records are sealed for the Head Curator') frame stamping as filing, not being graded, but hesitation latency is logged, not soothed away with correctness promises.
Rotation mistaken for the task itself: she may spin solids expecting something to unlock. The pulsing clipboard and the disabled-until-selected stamp keep the real required action visible.

Believing the amber dim means 'wrong': the identical reaction to every stamp, established from item one, is the defense; if she verbally probes ('was that right?'), the instrument gives no signal by design.
instrumentRisks: Rotation could over-help I4: seeing the square base by turning the pyramid converts silhouette reasoning into direct observation. I accept this deliberately — the contract's C4 statement targets reasoning from the actual face set, and rotation is uniform affordance, not per-item scaffolding — but I log rotationEngagedBeforeAnswer per item so an analyst can condition I4 evidence on whether the base was viewed. If the analyst rules this contaminates C4, the fix is locking I4 to the contract's fixed three-quarter view; I flag both options and commit to logging either way.

Idle auto-turn is a borderline exposure: it shows hidden faces without child action. Same logging (autoRevealOccurred) makes it auditable; it can be disabled per-item by configuration without redesign.

The seal-and-silence design may read as coldness to a hint-seeking child (her evidence shows she requests hints when stuck); risk is mid-evaluation disengagement. The reread button gives her a legitimate help-seeking act that costs nothing and is honestly logged.
Elimination-based success on I1 and I4 remains possible (contract-acknowledged); latency and optionChangeCount are the only mitigations available to me and are captured.
Narration of option cards could impose ordering salience (first-read primacy); card order is randomized per option list within contract fidelity, and displayed order is logged as optionOrderShown.

Glyphs beside shape-name options could theoretically aid a child who cannot read but also cannot match glyph-to-face — that would inflate C2. I judge the reading-confound removal worth it, and the contract's vocabulary-isolation follow-up is the designated resolver.
Fiction pressure ('before morning') could be read as a real timer and induce rushing; the clock visibly advances only on stamps, and the idle nudge explicitly says 'take your time'.
input.engagementPrediction: Prediction: Reina completes all five exhibits in a single 6–10 minute sitting with zero or one skip, engages rotation on at least three items, and uses the reread button at most twice — because her evidence shows she persists through difficulty when the task respects her (she asked for harder riddles) and she values clarity and visible color, both of which this design provides. I further predict the sealed-record fiction preempts frustration at the absence of feedback: she will accept 'sealed for the Head Curator' as a fair rule the way she accepted riddle rules, and will ask what her results were only after the shift report — a question the report answers factually.
falsifyingEvidence: If she abandons before I3 (the highest-reading multi-select), my bet that the museum fiction sustains a feedback-free five-item run is wrong, and the shell — not the items — failed her.
If she repeatedly taps sealed cards or asks 'was I right?' with visible distress, the sealed-ledger fiction did not make the silence legible and the honesty framing needs redesign.

If optionChangeCount spikes with near-zero rotation on I4, my claim that rotation is the natural instrument of face-set reasoning is falsified — she is treating this as a flat quiz and the 3D affordance added cost without evidentiary value.
If she stamps I1 in under ~3 seconds without rotating or scanning, engagement is compliance-shaped guessing and my dignity-through-fiction hypothesis produced speed, not reasoning.

If the reread button is pressed seeking content help and she stalls after receiving only format restatement, my substitution of format-help for her demonstrated hint-seeking style was insufficient, and the no-content-hint policy manifested as a trap-feeling even though no trap exists.

If I3/I5 show single-pin responses despite the changed header and pin tray, my visual multi-select signaling failed and under-selection data is instrument noise, not child evidence — the contract's format-burden control becomes mandatory, not optional.
If she disengages precisely at the payoff (ignores the lit museum and shift report), my prediction that factual completion is a sufficient reward for this child is falsified.
measurementResponsibilities: Log per item, exactly as contracted: selectedOption or selectedOptionSet, correct or exactSetCorrect, partialCreditPattern (I3), overSelectionCount/underSelectionCount/sphereSelected (I5), latencyMs (prompt-visible to stamp), optionChangeCount (pre-stamp toggles), hintRequested (reread presses).
Log design-added auditing keys clearly separated from contract keys: idleNudgeShown, rotationEngagedBeforeAnswer, autoRevealOccurred, optionOrderShown, narrationPlayed, skipUsed, exitPoint.
Record skips as noResponse (never scored incorrect) and unreached items as notAdministered, exactly per completion rule.
Guarantee zero correctness signaling in any channel — visual, motion, sound, narration — verified by an audit that the post-stamp event stream is byte-identical for correct and incorrect responses.
Enforce exposure integrity: each item rendered once, no re-entry after stamping, sealed cards never reveal content, replay path structurally cannot present I1–I5 again.
Honor I5's carryover annotation: emit the contract's conditional-evidence flag when I2 was answered correctly, so downstream scoring treats I5 as conditional C3 evidence.

Output the shift report and the analyst report with only factual language: attempts, assistance (hintRequested, idleNudgeShown), exposure (rotation/auto-reveal), possible confounds observed (single-pin multi-select, sub-3s latencies), friction events, and completion state — with per-construct status limited to provisional-support, provisional-gap, or indeterminate, and an explicit no-mastery-claim line.
